E7: BJT small-signal analysis II: every configuration, loading, and your Prac 3 (T6)

Why this matters in the exam: Small-signal BJT analysis is the largest block of WS6. Q3 to Q10 are all “find , , , ” questions, and the Week 5 slides spend slides 36 to 52 on it. The practice test gives AC analysis only 1 mark (MCQ V), because it stops at DC bias. The final is a different matter. The Week 7–8 FET amplifiers use exactly the same method (DC first, AC equivalent, read off , , , then load it), so this skill is worth marks twice. Expect at least one 8–12 mark question of the form “for the network shown, determine , , and , then with and find and ”.

E6 covered , , , , the hybrid-π and models, CE fixed bias and voltage-divider bias with bypassed. This pack covers everything else.

1. The core ideas

1.1 One idea that drives every formula: impedance reflection

In the model the base current is and the emitter current is . Two rules follow, and every result in this pack comes from them.

Looking into… You see Why
the base, with resistance in the emitter carries times the base current, so it looks times bigger from the base
the emitter, with resistance in the base the reverse: base-side resistance looks times smaller from the emitter
  • When to use: the first rule gives for the unbypassed CE and the emitter follower. The second gives for the emitter follower when there is a source resistance.
  • Trap: only the resistance in the signal path counts. A bypassed resistor is a short at signal frequency, so it is not reflected.

1.4 Emitter follower (common collector) (slide 42)

Output is taken from the emitter. The collector goes straight to , which is AC ground.

  • What it is for: buffering. It has a high and a low , and no voltage gain, but a large current gain.
  • Trap 1: the slide gives . That assumes the source is ideal (). When the follower is driven from (or from the collector of a previous stage), the source resistance is reflected as . That often doubles or more.
  • Trap 2: with a load, is in parallel with in the emitter, so it is reflected into . depends on : use .

1.5 Common base (slide 43)

Input at the emitter, output at the collector, base at AC ground.

  • When to use: the signal enters at the emitter and the base is grounded (WS6 Q4, Q7).
  • Trap: a CB stage has a huge but is only a few tens of ohms. Any real source resistance divides most of the signal away: with and keeps about 1.3 % of the gain.
  • Trap: CB is non-inverting. No minus sign.

1.6 Collector feedback (slide 44)

runs from collector to base. It sets the DC bias (E6/Week 4) and it is also an AC feedback path.

The Miller view (easier to remember and to extend to ). connects input to output, and the output is times the input, inverted. The voltage across is , so from the base it looks like a much smaller resistor:

With this gives the same number as the slide formula to within 0.3 % (Worked example 3).

  • When to use: whenever a resistor goes from collector to base with no capacitor in it.
  • Trap: depends on the gain, so depends on . With a load, use in the Miller formula.
  • Trap: the WS6 Q8 solution uses , which ignores at the output. The slide 44 formula keeps it. See Worked example 3.

2. The method

2.1 Recognise the configuration (10 seconds)

  1. Where does the signal go in? Base → CE or follower. Emitter → common base.
  2. Where does it come out? Collector → CE or CB. Emitter → follower.
  3. What is in the emitter at signal frequency? Nothing (grounded or fully bypassed) → type gain. A resistor → unbypassed, reflect it. Part of a resistor → partially bypassed.
  4. Is there a resistor from collector to base? → collector feedback (Miller).

  5. : find by reflection (×β), then put the bias resistors in parallel. For collector feedback, use Miller with the gain you will use.
  6. : set and look back into the output. CE/CB: (and only for the bypassed CE). Follower: . Collector feedback: .
  7. : quote the formula, substitute, write the sign and say “180° phase shift” or “in phase”.
  8. Loading: (Method A, or Method B where it is exact), then , then if asked.
  9. Sanity check: . A follower gain is just under 1. An unbypassed gain is close to .

4. Traps that cost marks

  • Skipping the DC analysis. comes from . A wrong Q-point makes every AC answer wrong. Write the Q-point first, even if the question starts at “find ”.
  • Using the bypassed formula when is unbypassed (or using all of in AC when only is unbypassed). Look for the capacitor across before you write anything.
  • Forgetting the bias resistors in . is the transistor alone. (or ).
  • Writing for a follower driven from a real source. Add to .
  • Keeping the unloaded for a loaded follower or collector-feedback stage. In both, changes .
  • Sign and phase. CE and collector feedback are negative (180°). CB and the follower are positive. A loaded gain larger than the unloaded one means a sign or reciprocal slip.
  • Ignoring without saying why. Write “, so ignored”. If , include in the bypassed CE gain.
  • CB gain without the source divider. is tiny, so is a small fraction of unless is only a few ohms.

WS6 Q11 (course question). Typical speakers incorporate a solenoid (inductor) to actuate a membrane. The solenoid exhibits a very low DC resistance, e.g., less than 1 Ω. Having learned about AC coupling, the student in the previous Example modifies the design to that shown in figure 11 and attempts to drive a speaker. Unfortunately, the circuit still fails. Explain why. How can we resolve the issue?

Solution

Why it fails. The speaker is connected directly from the collector of to ground. At DC its solenoid is almost a short (under 1 Ω), so it pulls the collector to ground: . With , , so is driven into deep saturation and no longer works as an amplifier. The input coupling capacitor fixed the base bias, but the output is still DC-coupled.

Fix. Insert a coupling capacitor between the collector of and the speaker. It blocks the DC component while passing the AC signal, so the speaker no longer disturbs the bias, and the microphone signal is still amplified.

7. Add to your open-book reference sheet

SMALL-SIGNAL BJT II  (always: DC Q-point -> IE -> re = 26 mV/IE)
Reflection: R in emitter looks (b+1)R from base;  R at base looks R/b from emitter.

CE unbypassed:  Zb = b re + (b+1)RE ~ b(re+RE);  Zi = R1||R2||Zb;  Zo = RC
                Av = -RC/(re+RE) ~ -RC/RE   (no beta -> stable), 180 deg
Partial bypass: DC uses RE1+RE2;  AC uses RE1 only:  Av = -RC/(re+RE1)
Emitter foll.:  Zi = RB||b(re+RE||RL)  (RL changes Zi!)
                Zo = RE||re (ideal source);  Zo = RE||(re + (Rs||RB)/b) with Rs
                Av = RE/(RE+re) ~ 1, AvL = (RE||RL)/(RE||RL + re), in phase
Common base:    Zi = RE||re ~ re (tiny);  Zo = RC;  Av = aRC/re (in phase);  Ai = -a
Coll. feedback: Av = -(RC||RF)/re  [= -(RF/(RC+RF))RC/re];  Zo = RC||RF
                Zi = re/(1/b + RC/(RC+RF))  =  b re || RF/(1-Av)  (Miller; use AvL if loaded)
Loading:        AvL = AvNL * RL/(RL+Zo)   (two-port; exact for CE types only)
                CE: replace RC by RC||RL.   Avs = Zi/(Zi+Rs) * AvL.   AiL = -AvL*Zi/RL
                |AvNL| > |AvL| > |Avs|  always
ro: ignore only if ro >= 10RC (say so). Bypassed CE: Av = -(RC||ro)/re.
Prac measurement: Zi = Rs Vi/(Vs-Vi);  Zo = (VoNL - VoL)/VoL * RL
